title: If You Bought Your First House in 1956, This Is What It Cost

scenes.text: It's the spring of nineteen fifty-six. You're twenty-seven years old. You've been married for four years, and you have two little kids. For the last few years, you've been living in a cramped apartment over a shoe store, or in your in-laws' spare bedroom. And this Sunday, you and your wife are going to drive out to look at houses. Your very first house.
scenes.query: 1950s young couple looking at new house
scenes.caption: SPRING, 1956

scenes.text: Millions of young Americans made that same drive in the fifties. Between nineteen forty and nineteen sixty, the share of American families who owned their home jumped from about forty-four percent to about sixty-two percent. It was one of the biggest changes in American life, and it happened in about twenty years.
scenes.caption: 44% TO 62%

scenes.text: So what did it actually cost to buy your first house in nineteen fifty-six? How did you pay for it? What did you get? And how does it compare with today? Let's walk through it, from the model home to the moving van.
scenes.caption: WHAT DID IT COST?

scenes.text: First, a little background. During the Great Depression and the Second World War, almost no new houses were built for regular families. When the soldiers came home in nineteen forty-five and forty-six, there was a terrible housing shortage. Young couples lived in basements, attics, garages, trailers and old army barracks. Millions of them were desperate for a home of their own.
scenes.caption: THE HOUSING SHORTAGE

scenes.text: On Sunday afternoons, young couples drove out to the new developments at the edge of town. Builders put up a model home, furnished and decorated, with flags and balloons out front. There might be free coffee and doughnuts, and a salesman in a suit waiting to show you around.
scenes.caption: THE MODEL HOME

scenes.text: The houses were simple. A ranch house or a Cape Cod, usually one story, on a small lot. Two or three bedrooms, one bathroom, a living room, and a kitchen big enough for a table. In nineteen fifty, the average new single-family house was only about a thousand square feet. By the late fifties, it was getting a little bigger.
scenes.caption: 1,000 SQUARE FEET

scenes.text: But to a young couple who had grown up in the Depression, it looked like a palace. A brand-new kitchen with modern appliances. A yard for the kids. A driveway. Closets. A house that nobody else had ever lived in. Many couples signed the papers that same afternoon.
scenes.caption: IT LOOKED LIKE A PALACE

scenes.text: Builders had learned to build fast. William Levitt, the most famous of them, built houses like an assembly line. Trucks dropped materials at each lot, and teams of workers moved from house to house, each doing one job. At the peak, his crews in Levittown, New York, finished around thirty houses a day.
scenes.caption: 30 HOUSES A DAY

scenes.text: So what was the price? In nineteen fifty-six, a basic new house in a development might cost between ten and fifteen thousand dollars. The median value of a home in the nineteen sixty census was about eleven thousand nine hundred dollars. Some small houses sold for less than ten thousand.
scenes.caption: AROUND $12,000

scenes.text: That sounds unbelievably cheap today. But let's put it in perspective. In nineteen fifty-six, the median family income in America was about four thousand eight hundred dollars a year. So a typical house cost about two and a half times what a family earned in a year.
scenes.caption: 2.5 YEARS OF INCOME

scenes.text: Today, the median house price in America is around five to six times the median household income, and in many cities much more. That's the real difference. It's not just that the numbers were smaller. A house in nineteen fifty-six cost far less, compared with what people earned.
scenes.caption: THEN AND NOW

scenes.text: Few families could pay cash, so they got a mortgage. And here, the government had made a huge difference. Before the nineteen thirties, a home loan usually lasted five to ten years, and you might need to put down half the price. Many loans ended with a big payment that families couldn't make.
scenes.caption: BEFORE THE 1930S

scenes.text: The Federal Housing Administration, created in nineteen thirty-four, changed all that. It insured long-term mortgages of twenty or thirty years, with small down payments. Suddenly, a monthly payment could be about the same as rent. Banks were willing to lend, because the government stood behind the loans.
scenes.caption: THE FHA

scenes.text: And for veterans, there was the G.I. Bill. Signed in nineteen forty-four, it guaranteed home loans for returning soldiers, often with no down payment at all. By the mid-fifties, millions of veterans had used it to buy homes. Many young men who had grown up in rented rooms became homeowners before they turned thirty.
scenes.caption: THE G.I. BILL

scenes.text: Mortgage interest rates in the mid-fifties were around four and a half to five percent. On a twelve thousand dollar house, with a small down payment and a thirty-year loan, the monthly payment might be around sixty to seventy dollars, plus taxes and insurance. For many families, that was less than they'd been paying in rent.
scenes.caption: ABOUT $70 A MONTH

scenes.text: Getting the loan was personal. You sat across a desk from a loan officer at the local bank or savings and loan, in your best suit. He asked about your job, how long you'd held it, and whether you had any debts. A steady job at the plant and a good reputation in town counted for a lot. The whole thing was done on paper, with carbon copies.
scenes.caption: THE LOAN OFFICER

scenes.text: But not everyone could get that deal. For decades, federal housing agencies and banks refused to insure or lend in neighborhoods where Black families lived, a practice known as redlining. Many new developments, including Levittown, had rules that kept Black families out entirely.
scenes.caption: NOT EVERYONE

scenes.text: The Supreme Court ruled in nineteen forty-eight that those racial rules in property deeds could not be enforced by courts. But discrimination in housing continued for years, and it wasn't outlawed until the Fair Housing Act of nineteen sixty-eight. For millions of families, the dream of a first house in the fifties stayed out of reach.
scenes.caption: OUT OF REACH

scenes.text: For the families who did buy, moving day was a big adventure. Many couldn't afford a moving company, so they borrowed a truck from a friend, or loaded everything into the car and made a dozen trips. Brothers, cousins and friends from work helped carry the furniture.
scenes.caption: MOVING DAY

scenes.text: And there often wasn't much furniture to move. A bed, a kitchen table and chairs, a couch from a relative, and a few boxes of dishes. Many new homeowners had empty rooms for months, or even years. Living rooms with only a couch and a television, and a bedroom with a mattress on the floor.
scenes.caption: EMPTY ROOMS

scenes.text: The first night in the new house was unforgettable. Children ran from room to room, claiming bedrooms. Parents sat on the front steps, looking out at the street, hardly believing it was theirs. Some couples remember eating sandwiches on the kitchen floor, because the table hadn't arrived yet. And many say it was one of the happiest nights of their lives.
scenes.query: 1950s family new house front steps evening
scenes.caption: THE FIRST NIGHT

scenes.text: The neighborhood was often brand new too. Mud instead of grass. Little sticks where trees would someday be. No sidewalks yet, sometimes no paved streets. But all around you were young couples just like you, moving in the same month, with kids the same age.
scenes.caption: MUD INSTEAD OF GRASS

scenes.text: Once you had the house, you had to fill it. And the American economy was ready. Families bought refrigerators, washing machines, vacuum cleaners and televisions, often on installment plans. A few dollars down and a few dollars a month. Sears, Montgomery Ward and the local furniture store all offered credit.
scenes.caption: A FEW DOLLARS A MONTH

scenes.text: A new refrigerator in nineteen fifty-six might cost around two hundred to three hundred dollars. A television, about the same. A washing machine, maybe two hundred. Those were big purchases, a month or two of a man's pay. Many families bought one thing at a time, paying off the last one before buying the next.
scenes.caption: ONE THING AT A TIME

scenes.text: And many husbands became handymen. They built shelves, painted rooms, put up fences, finished the basement, and planted the lawn and the trees. Hardware stores boomed. Do-it-yourself became a national hobby. A man's Saturday belonged to the house.
scenes.caption: DO IT YOURSELF

scenes.text: And then there was the lawn. In the fifties, the lawn became a symbol of a good homeowner. Men spent their weekends seeding, watering, fertilizing and mowing. Push mowers, and then gas-powered rotary mowers, buzzed up and down the street every Saturday morning. A brown, weedy lawn could get you a talking-to from the neighbors.
scenes.caption: THE LAWN

scenes.text: What was it like to live there? For many families, wonderful. Children played in the street until dark, in packs of a dozen or more. Mothers met over the back fence. Neighbors had barbecues and cocktail parties. On summer nights, everyone sat out on their lawn chairs and talked.
scenes.caption: CHILDREN IN PACKS

scenes.text: The new suburbs needed everything. New schools, new churches, new shopping centers, new parks and new roads. Many of the first homeowners joined the PTA, the church building committee, the Little League and the volunteer fire department. They built not just houses, but whole communities.
scenes.caption: BUILDING COMMUNITIES

scenes.text: There were problems too. Some of the houses were built very quickly, and cheaply. Basements leaked. Walls were thin. And for wives without a car, the new suburbs could feel very far from everything. But most families who bought in the fifties never regretted it.
scenes.caption: BUILT QUICKLY

scenes.text: Taxes were another thing to plan for. Property taxes paid for the new schools, and as the suburbs filled with children, those taxes rose. Many families also paid for homeowners insurance, water and sewer service, and garbage pickup for the first time. Being a homeowner meant a whole new list of bills, kept in a shoebox or a little file box on the kitchen counter.
scenes.caption: A NEW LIST OF BILLS

scenes.text: And here's the remarkable part. For many families, that first house became the most valuable thing they ever owned. A house bought for twelve thousand dollars in nineteen fifty-six might be worth twenty or thirty times as much today. It paid for college, helped with retirement, and was passed down to children.
scenes.caption: THE MOST VALUABLE THING

scenes.text: Many of those families paid off their thirty-year mortgage in the mid-eighties. Some held mortgage-burning parties, literally setting the paid-off papers on fire in the backyard grill, with friends and neighbors cheering. It was the end of a long road, and a proud moment.
scenes.caption: THE MORTGAGE-BURNING PARTY

scenes.text: And many of those houses are still there today. Levittown, New York. Lakewood, California. Park Forest, Illinois. Thousands of suburbs all over the country. The houses have been expanded, remodeled and repainted, but you can still see the simple fifties shape underneath.
scenes.caption: STILL THERE TODAY

scenes.text: Compare that with buying a first home today. The average first-time buyer in America is now in their mid-thirties, older than ever before. In nineteen fifty-six, many first-time buyers were in their twenties. Today, a down payment alone can take years to save, and in many cities, a small starter house costs hundreds of thousands of dollars.
scenes.caption: OLDER THAN EVER

scenes.text: That doesn't mean life in the fifties was easy. Families worked hard, saved hard, and did without a lot of things. But a young working family really could buy a house on one paycheck. It was one of the great achievements of postwar America, and many people today wish it were still possible.
scenes.query: 1950s father coming home from work house
scenes.caption: ONE PAYCHECK

scenes.text: If your parents bought their first house in the fifties, you might remember the stories. The tiny kitchen. The empty living room. The day the grass finally grew. And maybe you remember the day they paid it off. It was more than a house. It was the American dream, made real.
scenes.caption: THE DREAM MADE REAL

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. When did your family buy its first house, and what did it cost? Do you remember the address? Is it still standing? We read every comment. Next time, we're counting twenty-five things every nineteen sixties living room had. Thank you for spending this time with me.
scenes.caption: WHAT DID YOUR HOUSE COST?
